hansard.speaker: Baroness Sugg (Con)
hansard.text: My Lords, I fully recognise the importance of high-quality data and the need for healthcare services to learn from outcomes and continuously improve patient safety—and, of course, for women to have access to accurate information. Indeed, better data collection in women's health is something I strongly support. I am grateful to my noble friend Lord Moylan for his introduction and explanation of the Bill. However, I remain unconvinced that the Bill is the right way to achieve those outcomes. As the House of Lords Library briefing notes, abortion complications are already recorded, abortion statistics are already published annually, and there is already a statutory framework requiring notification and reporting of relevant information. The question before us is not whether data should be collected but whether abortion alone should be singled out in primary legislation for a dedicated annual report. When we last debated the Bill in December 2024, the Minister argued that abortion is a safe procedure and no other area of healthcare has a legislative requirement of this kind for the publication of complication reports. As we have heard, the evidence before us continues to show that abortion is a very safe procedure and complications are rare, as set out in the briefing from the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists. That briefing also warns that the Bill risks stigmatising both women accessing abortion care and the healthcare professionals who provide it. The college further argues that decisions around clinical practice and patient safety should be led by medical evidence and clinical expertise, rather than through primary legislation. Developments since our previous debate have strengthened rather than weakened the case against the Bill. The House of Lords Libra

hansard.speaker: Baroness Bennett of Manor Castle (GP)
hansard.text: There was a Committee stage as well. The Green Party and I oppose the Bill, and I make no apology for situating it in the undeniable context of the extremely well-funded campaign, originating chiefly in America but felt around the world, against women's right to reproductive healthcare. This is driven by disturbing anti-female ideology. As I said at the last Second Reading, this is a long-running campaign. The success of that campaign in the US has had awful impacts on the health of American women, as the noble Baroness, Lady Brinton, outlined. Predictably, those who are subject to economic and social disadvantage suffer the most. The wealthy will always find a way to access abortion and, most usually, a safe method of abortion. However, I want to be positive and note that this debate is happening in a context where we can celebrate real progress in the UK. Not only have we seen come into force a legal amendment that prevents women being criminalised for ending their own pregnancies, but it has also delivered pardons for about 150 women who were affected by that law. I note, however, that that law does not currently apply in Scotland. The Scottish Green Party is seeking to deliver in Scotland the same legal protection that women in England and Wales now have, as well as looking to a full decriminalisation of abortion so that it is treated like any other health procedure. It is worth looking at the history of this. We are celebrating the end of something, so let us go back to the start. I credit the Guardian with reporting this. What has happened over the centuries? In 1862, just after the law that was often used against women having abortions came in, Fanny Worboys, a widow, was injured in a back-street abortion and then sentenced to three months in prison as a result.

hansard.speaker: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Department of Health and Social Care (Baroness Merron) (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, I am grateful to the noble Lord, Lord Moylan, for his clear introduction of the points he seeks to pursue in this Bill. I am also grateful to noble Lords who have contributed to this debate, which follows on from one we had a few years ago, as noble Lords have referenced by way of Hansard . I will address the points that are for the Government. Parliament has determined the legal framework in respect of abortion, and the role of the Government is to ensure access to safe, legal abortion services within that framework. Of course, Parliament decides the circumstances in which abortion should be available. Any changes to the law—the noble Lord, Lord Weir of Ballyholme, spoke to this when he talked about debate and ranges of opinion—are rightly a matter for parliamentarians to decide. Abortion is an issue on which the Government adopt a neutral stance as a matter of conscience. The Government have expressed reservations about the Bill because, as the noble Lord, Lord Moylan, correctly predicted, as we agree with the noble Lord, Lord Kamall, and other noble Lords that legislation is not necessary to provide for the publication of an annual report. The aims of this Bill could be achieved through existing mechanisms, and there is no need for new legislation. Indeed, in 2023 the department published a report on abortion complications and retains the ability to publish further reports when appropriate. We do not currently plan to publish separate annual reports on abortion complications, as there is no operational requirement to do so. I am sure noble Lords will understand that all of us should avoid legislating where reasonable and effective alternative mechanisms are already available, as in this case. The department publishes annual abortion statistics in a report t

hansard.speaker: Lord Kamall (Con)
hansard.text: My Lords, before I start, I must ask myself why I volunteer to come in on Fridays. The last time I was in on a Friday, it was the assisted dying Bill, and now we have an abortion Bill. I should be more careful before volunteering to do Front-Bench duty. I thank my noble friend Lord Moylan for setting out the case for the Bill and all noble Lords, whatever their views, who spoke in this debate. As someone who studied engineering and maths and later worked with econometricians, noble Lords may realise that I am slightly geeky about the need for reliable data and statistics; in fact, the noble Baroness, Lady Freeman, has often pointed that out to me. Noble Lords will be aware that I often question the Minister on what data is collected in order to make better decisions and improve the standard of health and social care. The Bill itself calls for the publication of an annual report on complications from abortions. We have heard it said that, where possible, hospital episode statistics and abortion notification system complication rates should be collected, alongside those for incomplete abortions, in order to improve patient safety. As my noble friend Lord Moylan said, Parliament expressed its will that such data be reported confidentially and securely to the Chief Medical Officer, under Section 2 of the Abortion Act 1967, which gives effect to the Abortion Regulations 1991 that require doctors carrying out abortions to notify the relevant person of any complications that occurred during the course of an abortion. The law is therefore already clear that data relating to complications as a result of abortions should be collected and reported to the Minister for Health or the Chief Medical Officer. However, as many noble Lords have pointed out, since 1967, due to medical adva

hansard.speaker: Lord Moylan (Con)
hansard.text: My Lords, I am grateful to all noble Lords who have spoken in the debate, the great majority of whom engaged to some extent with the Bill. I will go through a few comments that were made. The noble Baronesses, Lady Thornton and Lady Sugg, and others, raised the question of abortion being exceptionalised by the Bill. I refute that. It is the case that abortion is treated exceptionally because of the 1967 Act. I do not know what was in the minds of parliamentarians in 1967 when they put the requirement for mandatory reporting in a statute—something that exists, I agree, but does not exist for other medical procedures—but they did so, and I am simply taking that for granted. Nobody has suggested removing it. It is perfectly legitimate to suggest removing it, but you need a different Private Member's Bill. It is not one that arises in relation to today. The noble Baroness, Lady Thornton, also said it was difficult to collect the statistics to which I am referring. It is more difficult to collect them than it might be if they were reported directly. The OHID had to go into hospitals to get the data, but data is already available, as the Minister said. It is recorded in hospital episode statistics by code—the NHS has a code for nearly every procedure it carries out. It would be less difficult to collect it if hospitals were simply required to report it on a routine basis. It would then be held centrally and could be gathered. It is not a difficult thing to do. The noble Baroness, Lady Brinton, misunderstood me in one respect. I said I thought that the HSA4 form is required for every termination, not only in the case of complications, so she is right about that. We are in strong agreement on the matter. As far as data is concerned, I did not say that 1.8%, or 2% if you prefer

hansard.speaker: Baroness Brinton (LD)
hansard.text: My Lords, it is my pleasure to follow the noble Baroness, Lady Thornton, who has laid out the arguments against the need for this Bill very clearly. I thank those who have briefed us, including the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, BPAS and the Library. I also thank the noble Lord, Lord Moylan, for his extensive explanation; I am afraid that he has not convinced me, but that may not surprise him. I will focus on data. Regulations issued under the Abortion Act require specifically that a woman's name and date of birth, or a personal identifier, be submitted on every abortion provided—not just on complications, as the noble Lord, Lord Moylan, implied earlier—to the Chief Medical Officer via the abortion notification system. It is important to note that NHS numbers are not required. That is important partly because, as has been outlined, some of the data on complications is collected before the patient is discharged from the clinic. That data, as we know, is managed by the Department of Health and Social Care. The second set of data, on hospital episode statistics, details activity that happens afterwards. The noble Lord referred to a woman at home having complications and ending up in A&E—that is a reassuring aspect of the data, because it does end up in the system; it may not be linked to the first dataset, but there is a reason for that. The noble Lord cited some statistics. He said that 18 per 1,000 was a very high percentage of complications; in fact, that is 1.8%. It is very similar to the US figures for abortions up to 24 weeks: complications account for 2.1%, with major complications accounting for only 0.3%. The results for complications are much lower than could be implied by hearing about the data cited by the noble Lord. Our concerns remain tha

hansard.speaker: Baroness Thornton (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, I first thank the noble Lord, Lord Moylan, for the clear explanation of his Bill. Of course, it is not the first time we have heard the noble Lord's exposition, and he has undertaken it with great detail and great research, even if I disagree with him from time to time. I do not disagree with the noble Lord in the comment he made about the change that there has been in the availability of abortion, particularly with the at-home pill and tele-abortion, and all to the better for women and their health. I thank the Library, BPAS and others for their briefing on the Bill. The noble Lord will not be surprised that I remain unconvinced by his speech—now as then—and of either the desirability or the necessity of this Private Member's Bill. I agree with BPAS and feel quite strongly that it is not desirable, in principle, because the creation of a law to require the reporting of complications in this way exceptionalises abortion and fails to treat it like other forms of healthcare, where reporting on NHS statistics is there. There is a danger of stigmatising both clinicians and women. I have to say that despite what the noble Lord has said, my suspicion is that this might be part of the motivation for those who are supporting the Bill. My noble friend the Minister said in December 2024, when the House last considered the Bill, that it is “a very safe procedure in which major complications are rare at all gestations”. My noble friend went on to say: “The aims of the Bill can be achieved through existing routes … and further legislation is unnecessary”.
